summary_html: A **court reverses or vacates** a CPS or agency decision due to procedural error, insufficient evidence, or constitutional violation. Federal review data (CFSR, ASFA) tracks judicial determinations on reasonable efforts and due process.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — judicial findings of 'reasonable efforts' compliance  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of judicial/agency conformity  
- **42 U.S.C. § 1983** — civil-rights remedy for unconstitutional removals (14th & 4th Amendments).

key_cases.case_name: E.R. v. Department of Children & Family Services
key_cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Third District
key_cases.holding: Termination of the father's parental rights was reversed because the trial court's order was not supported by competent substantial evidence, where the Department's own counselor testified he was not a danger to his children.
key_cases.relevance: E.R. is a Florida example of appellate reversal of a termination judgment for evidentiary insufficiency.
key_cases.quote: We reverse because the trial court's order is not supported by competent, substantial evidence.

key_cases.case_name: In re J.B. (J.B. v. Department of Children & Family Services)
key_cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Second District
key_cases.holding: An order placing children in permanent guardianship and terminating protective supervision was reversed because the procedure used did not produce an adequate evidentiary hearing on the facts required to support permanent guardianship.
key_cases.relevance: Ending supervision through a summary permanency procedure is reversible error.
key_cases.quote: the procedure used did not result in an adequate evidentiary hearing to establish the factual issues necessary to support an order of permanent guardianship

key_cases.case_name: Statewide Guardian ad Litem Office v. C.C.
key_cases.holding: An appellate court may not reweigh the evidence supporting a termination judgment; because competent substantial evidence supported the trial court's least-restrictive-means and manifest-best-interests findings after the father failed a voluntary case plan, the district court's reversal was quashed.
key_cases.relevance: It limits when a district court may reverse a dependency or termination judgment: not by reweighing evidence.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the Fifth District's decision improperly reweighed the evidence below and, thus, conflicts with our precedent.

key_cases.case_name: T.L. v. Department of Children & Families
key_cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Fourth District
key_cases.holding: The order denying the mother's motion for reunification and placing the children in permanent guardianship was reversed and the guardianship vacated because the finding that she had not substantially complied with her case plan lacked competent substantial evidence.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Florida remedy when a permanency order rests on evidence that does not support it.
key_cases.quote: We vacate the order of permanent guardianship and reverse and remand for a new hearing on the Mother's motion for reunification.

key_cases.case_name: M. L. B. v. S. L. J.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: A State may not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a decree terminating parental rights on her ability to advance record preparation fees; Mississippi had to furnish a record sufficient to permit appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence.
key_cases.relevance: M.L.B. guarantees that the appellate remedy for an erroneous termination judgment is actually available to an indigent parent, which is the precondition for the court-reversal route this node describes.
key_cases.quote: Mississippi may not deny M. L. B., because of her poverty, appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence on which the trial court found her unfit to remain a parent
